summary.text: A metabolic pathway is a linked series of chemical reactions inside a cell, where the product of one enzyme usually becomes the substrate for the next.
Anabolic pathways build molecules using energy, while catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy that the building pathways then use.
How much flows through a pathway is regulated by the needs of the cell and the availability of the substrate, which helps maintain homeostasis.

facts.label: Two main types
facts.value: Anabolic (builds with energy) and catabolic (breaks down)

facts.label: Amphibolic pathway
facts.value: Can be catabolic or anabolic, depending on energy need or availability

facts.label: Location matters
facts.value: Different pathways run in different parts of a eukaryotic cell

facts.label: Cycles
facts.value: Some pathways loop, as the Krebs cycle does

items.prompt: A cell builds a large, complex molecule out of smaller pieces. Where does the energy for that job come from?

options.label: From the building reactions themselves, which give off energy
From catabolic pathways, whose breakdown reactions provide it
From waste side products that the cell recycles at the end
From enzymes, which hand over energy when they bind

items.explain: The breakdown in a catabolic pathway provides the energy that an anabolic pathway uses for biosynthesis.

items.prompt: Enzyme one in a pathway makes a molecule. What usually happens to that molecule next?

options.label: It is removed from the cell as waste straight away
It is held back until the whole pathway has finished
It switches off the enzyme that made it every time
It serves as the substrate for the next enzyme in the pathway

items.explain: In most pathways the product of one enzyme is the substrate of the next, and only side products are treated as waste.

items.prompt: A cell's demand for a product rises and falls through the day. What changes in the pathway making it?

options.label: How much flows through it, set by cell needs and substrate supply
Its enzymes swap places so the pathway runs in a new order
The pathway splits into two copies, one for each shift
Nothing, because pathways always run at one fixed rate

items.explain: The flux of metabolites through a pathway is regulated depending on the needs of the cell and the availability of the substrate.

items.prompt: A cell has one pathway that makes a particular amino acid. How is that amino acid typically broken down?

options.label: By the same pathway running backward
By the same enzymes in reverse order
By a separate and distinct pathway
It cannot be broken down inside the cell

items.explain: Pathways are often considered to flow in one direction, so synthesis and breakdown of an amino acid usually use separate pathways.

items.prompt: Building and breaking down molecules can happen in the same eukaryotic cell. How are the two kept from getting in each other's way?

options.label: They run only at different hours of the day
They share every enzyme but use opposite temperatures
Each uses enzymes borrowed from neighbouring cells
Separate organelles, or different enzymes and co-factors

items.explain: Anabolic and catabolic pathways in eukaryotes are separated physically by compartments or biochemically by needing different enzymes and co-factors.

items.prompt: A eukaryotic cell is running fatty acid biosynthesis and the electron transport chain. How do their locations compare?

options.label: Both take place in the mitochondrial membrane
Biosynthesis is in the cytosol; the chain is in the mitochondrial membrane
Both take place in the cytosol of the cell
The chain is in the cytosol; biosynthesis is in the mitochondrial membrane

items.explain: Fatty acid biosynthesis occurs in the cytosol, while the electron transport chain takes place in the mitochondrial membrane.
